senses.gloss:
dharmameghasamādhi
(‘samādhi of the cloud of धर्म’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) is a well-known ancient treatise that deals with the art and science of concentration. This word ‘dharmameghasamādhi’ is a technical term used there in the sūtra 4.29.
Viveka (discrimination that the पुरुष or the सोउल्, who is of the nature of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, is separate and distinct from the प्रकृति or insentient nature) and वैराग्य (dispassion towards प्रकृति and its products) are the two basic disciplines that ultimately lead to the purification of the मिन्द् and consequent experience of oneself as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. When this is achieved through समाधि or perfect concentration, then even the seeds of old सṁस्कारस् or tendencies that might rise up and disturb the मिन्द्, are completely transcended.
But this experience of prasaṅkhyāna or knowledge that one is the conscious spirit, separate and different from the प्रकृति, may produce a sort of attachment to that state itself as also to the psychic powers that may result from it. However elevated it is, an attachment even to that state is to be overcome. The योगि who is not attracted even by this, attains ‘dharmameghasamādhi’. In this state his विवेकख्याति (knowledge or experience of his separateness from the insentient प्रकृति) is constant, continuous and permanent. Such a state is called ‘dharma-meghasamādhi,’ because it ‘rains’ on him, like the rainbearing cloud (= megha), the ‘dharma’ or the special quality of not being affected by any type of कर्म he does—because he is now a liberated person—which कर्म is aśukla-कृष्ण, neither white (good) nor black (bad), incapable of producing any fruits.
See also SAMĀDHI and YOGADARŚANA.

Dhāreśvara
------------------------------------------
Temples have exerted a great influence on the Hindu society for several centuries. Though the ancient temples built of perishable materials like wood, have disappeared due to the ravages of nature and time, those built of stones have survived. One such is the Pañca-keśvara temple—also known as Dorānātha temple—at the village धारेश्वर, near the town Kumaṭa in the North Kanara district of Karnataka. It is a beautiful temple built in the Cāḷukyan style. There is a nice tank just inside the main compound. There are also two ‘hero-stones’ (Vīragallu, a stone slab or pillar erected in honour of a hero who fought for the people) and a stone edict (A. D. 1083) containing the description of a gift by the local queen.
According to mythological accounts, when रावण, the demon king of लङ्का, was bringing the ātmaliṅga (śivaliṅga) from कैलास, it got stuck on the ground at गोकर्ण (in North Kanara, Karnataka). रावण could not dislodge the लिङ्ग from the ground but succeeded in pulling out the cloth and thread from it and threw it away. The thread fell at धारेश्वर and became a लिङ्ग.
There are many beautiful images in the area around धारेश्वर like those of नरसिṁह and Veṇugopāla. There is a broad road in front of the temple for the रथोत्सव or temple-car festival.

Dharmasindhu
(‘Ocean of धर्म’)
------------------------------------------
For over two millennia, Hindu society has been guided and regulated by a special class of literature known as the धर्म-śāstras. These works have prescribed rules of conduct for a person both at the individual and at the social level.
The dharmaśāstra literature has three aspects: the धर्मसूत्रस्, the smṛtis and the निबन्धस्.
The निबन्धस् are digests containing a lot of information on various aspects of धर्म and its application, culled from a number of authoritative sources.
The Dharmsindhu—also known as the Dharmasindhusāra or Dharmābdhi-sāra—of Kāśīnātha Upādhye, is a leading and popular work especially in the Maha-rashtra State, guiding Hindu religious observances. It might have been composed during the period A. D. 1790-91.
The book is divided into three paricchedas or sections. The topics dealt with in it may be summarised as follows:
divisions of the year, the seasons and the times considered auspicious or inauspicious for religious and social rites; sacraments like उपनयन and मर्रिअगे; आह्निक or the daily duties of a द्विज (a member of the first three castes); śrāddhas or obsequial rites.
It seems to have derived inspiration from another, better known, work called Nirṇayasindhu of कमलाकर (A. D. 1612).

dharmaśāstras
------------------------------------------
Introduction
The concept of धर्म and its appli-cation to the various aspects of life is of fundamental importance in हिन्दुइस्म्. The concept itself has undergone several changes over the centuries. As derived from the root ‘dhṛ’ (‘to support, to sustain’), the most general meaning of the word ‘dharma’ is ‘that which supports and sustains’. Gradually it came to acquire several senses such as—ordinance, usage, duty, right, justice, मोरलित्य्, virtue, reli-gion, good works, function or characteristic. However, the sense of ‘duties and responsibilities based on some fundamental moral virtues’ became most widely accepted.
Sources of Dharma
The वेदस् being the primary scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, naturally get the pride of place as the definer and the source of धर्म. But, with the growth of the human society and the consequent problems it had to face, there arose a great need to expand the scope of and to delve deeper into, the concept itself. It is this that gave rise to the composition of the later works, now included under the comprehensive term ‘dharmaśāstras.’
According to all these works, the sources of धर्म are: the वेदस्; the smṛtis; the teachings and conduct of persons who are well-versed in the scriptures and are of unblemished character; one’s own conscience.
Growth of the Dharmaśāstras
Though the वेदस् do not have positive precepts on matters of dharma—concerning personal conduct and social regulations as understood and defined by the later works, they do contain incidental references to various topics that fall under the domain of the धर्मशास्त्रस्. There are at least 50 passages in the वेदस् that shed light on the forms of मर्रिअगे, different kinds of sons, अदोप्तिओन् of a son, पर्तितिओन्, इन्हेरितन्चे, śrāddha ceremony and स्त्रीधन or property that should rightfully accrue to women. All these topics have been dealt with in much greater detail in the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
The first stage in the evolution of the धर्मशास्त्रस् is met with in the Vedāṅga (‘limb of the Veda’ or a subsidiary of the Veda) called ‘kalpasūtras.’ ‘Kalpa’ means procedure, the ‘how’ of a thing.
The कल्पसूत्रस् comprise four sections:
śrautasūtras;
gṛhyasūtras;
dharmasūtras and
śulbasūtras.
The first and the last are directly concerned with वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. Whereas the गृह्यसूत्रस् deal with the rites and ceremonies to be performed by a householder in his होउसे (gṛha = होउसे), the धर्मसूत्रस् are concerned with the more general and social aspects of धर्म, the conduct of human beings as members of a society, of a community. However, these two are interconnected and even inter-dependent.
In the गृह्यसूत्रस् and the धर्म-sūtras, the language is archaic and the delineation of the subjects is not very systematic. Hence the need arose for the composition of another class of works, now well-known as ‘smṛtis,’ written in a more intelligible language and mostly in poetical verses, to facilitate easy remembrance. Quite a few of these smṛtis are now available in print.
Though the धर्मसूत्रस् in general, are more ancient than the metrical smṛtis, it is equally possible that some from the latter group like the Manusmṛti, are as old as the former or even older. At least, the core-content could be so.
As the implementation of the rules of conduct in the society progressed, problems, including differences of opinion must have cropped up. Hence, commentaries on these works, attempting to expand the ideas given there or clear the doubts and anomalies, were written by competent scholars, thus enriching the whole field of dharmaśāstra literature.
As the number of such compositions increased, it became necessary to produce ready-reference material, containing abstracts, surveys and reviews, of all the matter available on that subject. This gave rise to another class of works known as ‘nibandhas’ or digests.
The two epics—the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata—as also many of the पुराणस् contain a lot of material that should normally be the concern of the धर्मशास्त्रस्. The निबन्धस्, naturally, have made good use of this material at the appropriate places.
Hence any standard work on the धर्मशास्त्रस् should avail of all the relevant stuff provided by these various sources.
Topics of the Dharmaśāstras
The topics generally dealt with in the धर्मशास्त्रस् fall under three broad groups: आचार (general conduct), vyavahāra (social conduct, law and order) and प्रायश्चित्त (expiatory rites for transgressions).
They may now be described briefly.
Ācāra
Unless the body-मिन्द् complex is kept clean and pure, both physically and ceremonially, a human being cannot attain धर्म in its two primary aspects, viz., अभ्युदय (worldly progress) and niśśre-yasa (spiritual welfare). This is achieved by strictly following आचार or the code of conduct, prescribed to be followed in one’s personal life. This code as ordained in the śruti (the वेदस्), the smṛtis (the secondary scriptures) and सदाचार (conduct of the sagely persons) should be practised meticulously, without indolence or neglect. सदाचार (good conduct) leads to long life, fulfilment of desires and attainment of wealth, whereas durācāra (bad and sinful conduct) results in disease, suffering, short-life and ill-fame.
The आचार or सदाचार concerns mainly what are termed as ‘ṣaṭkarmas’ or six daily rituals. They are: स्नान & सन्ध्या (bath and the सन्ध्या ritual), जप (repetition of Vedic mantras or God’s name), होम (oblations into a consecrated fire), devapūja (worship of gods), ātithya (entertaining the guests) and वैश्वदेव (offering cooked ड़ोओद् to all the gods).
Tarpaṇa or ceremonial offering of water with appropriate mantras, to देवस् (the gods), ṛṣis (sages) and पितृस् (manes) is also included in the daily routine.
Some aspects of these karmas like bath, worship of one’s family deity, repetition of the divine name and entertaining guests, apply to persons of all castes without any distinction.
As an important part of the ‘ācāra-kāṇḍa’ (section dealing with the ācāras), the ṣoḍaśasaṁskāras or 16 purificatory sacraments are also delineated. Upa-nayana (investiture with the sacred thread called ‘yajñopavīta’ and the imparting of the famous गायत्री-मन्त्र), विवाह (marriage) and अन्त्येष्टि (after-death ceremonies) are the most prominent of the 16 sacraments.
Another aspect of life, which is cardinal to Hindu religion and society, viz., the वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas, has also been given the primary place in all the dharmaśāstra works in the आचार section.
Vyavahāra
Though the word ‘vyavahāra’ refers to the general social conduct, in the धर्मशास्त्रस् it is used in a more technical sense, that of civil and criminal law.
In this section 18 subjects have been dealt with. Some of them are: ṛṇādāna (debts), sambhūya-samutthāna (partnership), saṁvid-vyatikrama (breach of contract), kraya-vikraya (purchase and sale), svāmi-pāla-vivāda (disputes between the master and the servant), sīmāvivāda (boundary disputes), daṇḍapāruṣya (assault), vākpāruṣya (libel), steya (theft), strīsaṅgrahaṇa (abduction of women), strīpuṁdharma (relation between husband and wife) and vibhāga (partition).
The king’s court was the judiciary. He was assisted by men of knowledge, wisdom and character in the dispensation of justice. He could also depute a judge to act on his behalf. There were duly appointed persons to oversee the implementation of the decisions taken by the court.
Prāyaścitta
To err is human. Human beings are prone to commit errors of omission and commission. If they do not realise their faults and mistakes, and do not reform themselves, they have to suffer a lot. This reformation has to be in two stages: repentance and a firm resolve that the mistake will not be repeated; expiation for the ones already committed.
The mistakes are called ‘pātaka or पाप’ (sin) and the expiations, ‘prāyaścitta’.
The प्रायश्चित्त sections of the धर्मशास्त्रस् describe the various types of sins, categorise them into महापातकस् (mortal sins) and upapātakas (venial sins) and prescribe the necessary expiations.
Sins like ब्रह्महत्या (killing a ब्राह्मण), सुरापान (drinking wine and other intoxicating liquids) and incest are classed among the महापातकस्. Minor sins like forsaking the sacred fires, offending the गुरु (Vedic teacher), minor thefts, non-payment of debts, selling prohibited articles, cutting down trees or killing harmless animals and so on, are grouped under upapātakas.
The prāyaścittas can vary from certain modes of तपस् (austerities) like ड़स्तिन्ग्, जप (repetition of certain Vedic formulae or names of God), दान (giving gifts), going on a पिल्ग्रिमगे (for minor sins), right up to religious सुइचिदे (for heinous sins).
The Philosophy of the Dharmaśāstras
The धर्मशास्त्रस् are not only based on the वेदस्, but, amplify their teachings for better application at day-to-day practical level. Of course, they do not forget to emphasise that the final goal of human life is the attainment of God who is one without a second, who is called by various names, who is the Supreme Ruler of the universe, the origin of च्रेअतिओन् and its final destination.
It is admirable that the धर्म-śāstras have recognised the importance of the physical body—its health, strength and energy as also its protection against dangers in times of emergency—as basic to any achievement in life, whether spiritual or temporal. Hence they advise everyone to protect his life and limb by all means at his disposal.
However, this is only the first step. Equally important is the cultivation of moral values. All the dharmaśāstra works, without exception, lay great stress on the सामान्य-dharmas or universal principles of truth, self control, decent and dignified behaviour (especially towards the women-folk), earning one’s livelihood by honest and right means, performing one’s duties and discharging the obligations to one’s family and the society, not harming others, personal and environmental cleanliness, study of (or listening to) sacred literature, a certain degree of austerity and devotion to God.
Some Important Dharmaśāstra Works
The dharmaśāstra literature (in Sans-krit) is very vast. Apart from the well-known works directly composed on the topics of the धर्मशास्त्रस्, there are innumerable verses spread over the two epics and the पुराणस् dealing with the various aspects of the subject. Here, an attempt will be made to give a very brief account of the more ancient and important of the works.
DHARMASŪTRAS
Āpastamba Dharmasūtras
This work forms the 28th and the 29th praśnas or sections of the bigger work, the Āpastamba Kalpasūtras. It belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. When compared with the Gṛhyasūtras of the same author, there are a few sūtras which are identical and the topics are inter-related. It may be assigned to the period 450-350 B. C. The style is more archaic and the sūtras are very concise.
A wide range of topics normally dealt with in the धर्मशास्त्रस् are found here also though the प्रायश्चित्त portion is more elaborate. One of its peculiarities is that it abounds in the technical terms and doctrines of the पूर्वमीमाṁसा school.
Auśanasa Dharmasūtras
Kāvya उशनस् is an ancient sage mentioned even in the Ṛgveda.
There is an Auśanasa Dharmaśāstra mostly in prose, available now, though in parts. The topics dealt with are: अशौच (impurity on birth and death), the four varṇas and some mixed castes, prāya-ścittas and śrāddha (obsequial rites).
The Auśanasa Dharmasūtras is in prose and contains material identical with that of some parts of the Manusmṛti. From the writings of other authors it is possible to assume that a bigger sūtra work was available, dealing with all the three aspects of आचार, vyavahāra and प्रायश्चित्त.
Another dharmaśāstra and also a स्मृति, both ascribed to उशनस् are available now either in print or in the manuscript form. The former has 51 verses and deals mainly with the mixed castes such as सूत and māgadha. The latter has 600 verses in 9 chapters and deals with such topics as उपनयन and śrāddha.
Baudhāyana Dharmasūtras
Baudhyāna probably lived during the period 600-300 B. C. and belonged to South India. His work on all the four branches of the कल्प are available now.
The Dharmasūtras is in 4 praśnas or khaṇḍas (sections). The subjects dealt with are: उपनयन, duties of a brahma-cārin, several purificatory rites, forms of मर्रिअगे, śrāddha ceremonies, सṁन्यास and some rites for securing सिद्धिस् or supernatural powers.
The Gṛhyasūtras deals mainly with the सṁस्कारस्.
Gautama Dharmasūtras
This ancient work is entirely in prose and can be assigned to the period 600-400 B. C. It has 28 chapters.
The topics dealt with are: details of the उपनयन for the various varṇas, the four āśramas, avocations of the four varṇas, सṁस्कारस् or sacraments, details of the duties of a king including च्रिमे अन्द् पुनिस्ह्मेन्त्, duties of women, prāyaścittas, rules of पर्तितिओन् of property and a few other minor topics.
Hārīta Dharmasūtras
Hārīta is considered as an ancient teacher since he has been quoted by आपस्तम्ब, बौधायन and वसिष्ठ. The work available now has thirty chapters. He speaks of eight kinds of marriages, of which kṣāttra and mānuṣa have replaced ārṣa and प्राजापत्य given in other works. He mentions two kinds of women, brahmavādinīs and sadyovadhūs, the former being entitled to undergo उपनयन, to the study of the वेदस् and even to the maintenance of Vedic fires.
This work may be assigned to the period 600-300 B. C.
Hiraṇyakeśi Dharmasūtras
This treatise forms the 26th and the 27th praśnas of the Kalpasūtras by Hiraṇyakeśin. It has borrowed profusely from the sūtra works of आपस्तम्ब and Bhāradvāja. Hence, it is not considered as an independent authority.
The author belonged to the Taittirīya school of Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and lived in the Konkan region (West Coast, South India).
Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtras
The work as available now, is a small one. It is also called Vaikhānasa-धर्म-praśna. It is considered as a later production, by a devotee of नारायण and may belong to the period A. D. 300-400. It could be a redaction of an earlier work.
It mentions four kinds each, of brahmacārins, gṛhasthas, vānaprasthas and saṁnyāsins.
Purification of golden and other metallic objects as also other things before their use, mentioned here seems to be interesting.
Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtras
Assigned to the period 300-100 B. C. this work is not a part of a kalpasūtra. It is very similar to the Dharmasūtras of बौधायन and गौतम.
The topics dealt with are almost the same as in other, similar, works. He mentions only six forms of मर्रिअगे, allows नियोग (levirate) and the remarriage of child-widows. Administration of justice by the king is another important subject dealt with.
Viṣṇu Dharmasūtras
This book professes to be a revelation of विष्णु in his Varāha or Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन्. It is said to belong to the Kaṭha school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It has a hundred chapters in mixed prose and verse, of which some parts are in common with the Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtras, popular in Kashmir.
It draws heavily on the Manusmṛti. राजधर्म (duties of a king), च्रिमे अन्द् पुनिस्ह्मेन्त्, twelve kinds of sons, mixed castes and ड़ुनेरल् रितेस् are some of the topics dealt with.
The date of the older part of this treatise is fixed as 300-100 B. C.
SMṚTIS
Aṅgirasa Smṛti
Aṅgiras is one of the ten primordial sages and has been mentioned even in the Ṛgveda.
Three smṛtis bearing his name have been published so far. The first one has 72 verses and is probably an abridgement. It deals mainly with prāyaścittas.
The second one has 168 verses, the subject being, again, prāyaścittas. It mentions some of the well-known authors of smṛtis like आपस्तम्ब, Śaṅkhalikhita and सुमन्तु.
The third one has 1200 verses and is different from the other two editions.
Atri Smṛti
Atri was an ancient writer on धर्म. Even मनु refers to him.
There is one Ātreya Dharmaśāstra available in 9 chapters. The work is in verses as well as in prose, in the sūtra form.
The topics dealt with are: gifts, prayers, austerities and expiations.
The work refers to a number of foreign tribes such as Śakas, यवनस्, Bāhlīkas and Paraśas.
There are other works styled Atri Smṛti or Atri Saṁhitā available in the manuscript form. They contain secret expiations for sins. They also deal with gifts and आचार.
Another Atri Saṁhitā, available in print has 400 verses and deals with the duties of the four castes.
Two more works—Laghu Atri and Vṛddha-आत्रेय Smṛti are also available.
Bṛhaspati Smṛti
Bṛhaspati was an ancient teacher of अर्थशास्त्र (economics and political science). He probably wrote a dharmasūtra work which is not available now. He has been quoted by several writers on the धर्मशास्त्रस्. Some writers consider him as an atheist.
The Bṛhaspati Smṛti available now has seven sections (mostly in verses) dealing with vyavahāra (social conduct), आचार (general conduct) including आपद्-धर्म (emergency measures) and प्रायश्चित्त.
He is assigned to the period A. D. 300-500.
Bṛhat-पराशर Smṛti
This is an extensive work of a late period, in 12 chapters comprising 3000 verses. It seems to be a recast of the Parāśara Smṛti by one Suvrata. The subjects dealt with are: षट्कर्मस् or six items of the daily routine, सṁस्कारस्, अशौच, prāyaścittas, duties of the four āśramas, राजधर्म (a king’s duties and responsibilities) and yogic disciplines.
Dakṣa Smṛti
This स्मृति is an old one. Printed texts have 220 verses distributed in seven chapters. The subjects treated are: the four āśramas, daily round of duties of the dvijas, various types of action, making gifts, अशौच, योग and its limbs, philosophies of the द्वैत and the advaita schools.
This स्मृति has been extensively quoted by others.
Devala Smṛti
Devala is a sage whose name often appears in the Mahābhārata, sometimes, along with another sage Asita. A धर्म-sūtra treatise—probably an extensive one—has been attributed to him. It perhaps contained sections on आचार, vyavahāra and śrāddha, as can be guessed by the numerous quotations in other works.
The Devala Smṛti available now seems to be a late work. It is in 90 verses and deals with purificatory rites.
Gobhila Smṛti
There is a gṛhyasūtra work of गोभिल belonging to the Sāmaveda. The Gobhila Smṛti available now has 491 verses in three sections. Topics like यज्ञोपवीत, उपाकर्म and śrāddha are dealt with in this work.
Kātyāyana Smṛti
Nārada, बृहस्पति and कात्यायन are the Trinity of sages considered as authorities in ancient Hindu Law. His work as available now has 973 verses (with an addenda of another 121 verses). Portions of the work on the vyavahāra section are yet to be recovered. He might have lived during the period 4th to 6th cent. A. D.
Another work, also attributed to कात्यायन is available in 3 sections comprising 29 chapters and about 500 verses. The contents are: details of wearing the sacred thread, worship of गणेश and the various goddesses in religious rites, some information connected with वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, chanting of Vedic mantras, śrāddha and अशौच.
Manusmṛti
The Manusmṛti is the most ancient and authoritative among the extant metrical treatises on धर्म. It has 12 chapters and 2684 verses, covering all the three aspects of a typical dharmaśāstra as follows: आचार (chs. 1-7), vyavahāra (chs. 8-10) and प्रायश्चित्त (chs. 11 & 12).
The topics dealt with include: च्रेअतिओन् of the world, four āśramas, the sixteen सṁस्कारस्, śrāddha, the four varṇas (castes), disputes and their resolution, āpad-dharmas (conduct during emergencies), the mortal sins and their expiation, good and bad deeds as also the nature of the आत्मन्.
The extant work may be assigned to the period 300 B. C. It may have undergone quite a few redactions.
Nārada Smṛti
The printed edition of this work has 21 chapters and 1028 verses. It was probably composed during A. D. 100-300.
It follows the Manusmṛti closely. It has been quoted by a few authors of निबन्धस्. The contents are generally the same as in the other धर्मशास्त्रस्. नारद differs from मनु in some respects and has introduced many sub-divisions in the major topics. His classification of impotent persons, women who can remarry, as also some of the juristic and political principles distinguish it from other works.
Parāśara Smṛti
Though पराशर was an ancient sage, the present work available in print must be a product of several revisions. The Parāśara Smṛti is said to be the ideal guide for this कलियुग or the Iron-age. It has 12 chapters and 592 verses. It deals only with आचार and प्रायश्चित्त.
The contents are: the four युगस्, the six daily duties, Vedic study, duties of a householder, the four varṇas and their duties, remarriage of widows under certain conditions, purification of various articles of use and expiations of various types for sins.
Two more works—the Bṛhat-Parāśara and the Vṛddha-Parāśara—are also available which are obviously later compositions.
Saṁvarta Smṛti
The Saṁvarta Smṛti as available in print today has 230 verses. It contains very ancient material. The extant work may be an epitome of the original स्मृति. It is in the form of teaching given by the sage Saṁvarta to वामदेव and other sages.
Its main contents are: rules of conduct for the ब्रह्मचारिन्; prāyaścittas for lapses on the part of the ब्रह्मचारिन् and others; duties of householders, forest hermits and मोन्क्स्.
Other authors have referred to the views of Saṁvarta on topics of vyavahāra by quoting him.
Vyāsa Smṛti
There is a स्मृति ascribed to व्यास and is available now. It has four chapters and 250 verses. It can be assigned to the period A. D. 200-500.
The contents can be summarised as follows: authoritativeness of the Śruti, the स्मृति and the पुराणस्; the sixteen सṁस्कारस्; mixed castes; duties of a ब्रह्मचारिन्; मर्रिअगे; नित्य (obligatory) naimittika (occasional) and kāmya (desire-motivated) karmas; eulogy of the householder stage and a few other related topics.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti
Yājñavalkya is a highly respected and one of the most brilliant and outstanding sages of ancient India. The Śukla Yajurveda was revealed to him.
The स्मृति that goes in his name now, has 1010 verses distributed among the three kānḍas or sections dealing with all the three topics: आचार, vyavahāra and प्रायश्चित्त. The whole work is well-organised and is in the classical anuṣṭubh metre.
The subjects dealt with can be briefly stated as follows: सṁस्कारस्, मर्रिअगे, वर्ण and जाति, दान, śrāddha, details of civil disputes and the methods of solving them, च्रिमे अन्द् पुनिस्ह्मेन्त्, अशौच and prāyaścittas as also some miscellaneous topics.
The original text must have undergone several revisions. The present form probably belongs to the period 100 B. C. to A. D. 300.
Yama Smṛti
Yama was probably a great sage since his views have been quoted even in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtras.
The extant स्मृति has 78 verses dealing with प्रायश्चित्त and शुद्धि (purificatory rites).
It is interesting to note that he prescribes punishment for cutting trees, shrubs, plants and creepers, especially if they have flowered or have fruits!
NIBANDHAS
Caturvargacintāmaṇi
This is an encyclopaedic work by हेमाद्रि on ancient religious rites and observances. It might have been composed during the period A. D. 1260-1270. Four volumes containing 6000 verses have so far been printed. The complete work has not been recovered till now. The four पुरुषार्थस् form the main content of the work. The topics of vrata (religious rites and observances), दान (gifts), śrāddha (obsequial ceremonies) and kāla (time and proper periods for the observance of religious rites) have been dealt with in great deal.
Kalpataru
The Kalpataru or the Kṛtya-kalpataru of लक्ष्मीधर is a voluminous work in fourteen kāṇḍas or Books. लक्ष्मीधर was a minister in the cabinet of the king Govindacandra of Kanauj (A. D. 1114-1154).
This treatise has exercised tremendous influence in North India for over 500 years.
The subjects dealt with in these fourteen kāṇḍas are: duties of brahma-cārins and gṛhasthas, आह्निक, śrāddha, vratas, पूजा (worship of gods), पिल्ग्रिमगे, prāyaścittas, शुद्धि, duties of a king, law and administration, शान्तिस् (propitiatory rites) and मोक्ष (liberation).
Nirṇayasindhu
An extensive and erudite work of कमलाकर भट्ट, this was probably composed around A. D. 1612. About a hundred smṛtis and three hundred authors of निबन्धस् have been named in this treatise.
The topics dealt with are: kāla, vratas, सṁस्कारस्, अग्निहोत्र, śrāddhas, kalivarjyas (actions forbidden in the कलियुग), अशौच and also सṁन्यास.
Smṛticandrikā
This is a well-known digest on the dharmaśāstra topics, by देवण्णभट्ट (circa A. D. 1150-1225), most probably from South India.
The contents are: वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas; सṁस्कारस्; daily duties of a द्विज; सन्ध्या, śrauta and smārta rites; rules about ड़ोओद्; the five daily sacrifices; procedure of law-courts; दायभाग; and śrāddhas.
Though several writers composed works styled Smṛticandrikā, it is only देवण्णभट्ट’s work that is held as authoritative and relied upon.
Smṛtikaustubha
Composed around the period A. D. 1645-1695 by Anantadeva (grandson of the famous Marathi saint and poet Eknāth), this vast digest deals with several topics such as: the sixteen सṁस्कारस्, rules for अदोप्तिओन्, festivals and sacred days, vāstu śāstra (architecture and town planning), चोरोनतिओन् of a king, homas and शान्तिस्.
Smṛtiratnākara
Caṇḍeśvara (circa A. D. 1314), the author of this extensive digest was a minister in the court of the king Bhaveśvara of मिथिला. This work is also known as the Ratnākara. It contains seven sections, each of them being called ‘Ratnākara’. They are: Kṛtyaratnākara, Dānaratnākara, Śuddhiratnākara, पूजा-ratnākara, Vyavahāraratnākara, Vivāda-ratnākara and Gṛhastharatnākara.
The subjects dealt with comprise the following areas: vratas, duties of होउसे-holders, various kinds of gifts, civil and criminal law, अशौच as also पूजा.
Smṛtitattva
This is the work of रघुनन्दन (A. D. 1510-1580), the last great writer of Bengal on the धर्मशास्त्रस्. It is divided into 28 sections, each being called ‘tattva’, such as Tithitattva, Durgāpūjātattva, Dāyatattva and so on. The topics delineated include—purificatory rites, sacraments, festivals like जन्माष्टमी and दुर्गोत्सव, civil law, public utility works, religious observances, establishment of temples, śrāddha and so on.
Vīramitrodaya
The Vīramitrodaya of Mitramiśra (circa A. D. 1610-1640) is a vast digest of धर्मशास्त्रस्, the second largest in size. Each of the sections is named as a ‘prakāśa,’ such as Vyavahāraprakāśa, Saṁskāraprakāśa, Rājanītiprakāśa and so on.
The contents include the following topics: आह्निक, पूजा, पिल्ग्रिमगे, civil law, सṁस्कारस्, राजनीति or political science, giving gifts, purificatory rites, śrāddha, prāyaścittas, भक्ति and मोक्ष.
Other Sources
Apart from the धर्मसूत्रस्, the smṛtis and the निबन्धस्, another factor that has contributed significantly to the enormous growth of this class of literature is the composition of learned commentaries on these works. These commentaries have explained the originals, expounded the various doctrines and subtle points and resolved many doubts and misgivings, thus giving a clear practical direction for implementing the various rules of the originals.
The following table gives some idea of these commentaries:
Commentaries of हरदत्त, Maska-rin and Asahāya on the Gautama Dharmasūtras.
Bhāṣyas (expositions) of मेधातिथि, Kullūka and five others on the Manusmṛti.
Bālakrīḍā of विश्वरूप, Mitākṣarā of विज्ञानेश्वर and Dikpālikā of शूलपाणि on the famous Yājñavalkya Smṛti.
Parāśara-mādhavīya by Mādhavā-cārya (Vidyāraṇya) and Vidvanmanoharā of नन्दपण्डित on the Parāśara Smṛti.
The Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (300 B. C.) along with its two commentaries Nayacandrikā of Mādhava Yajvan and Pratipadapañcikā of भट्ट Svāmin contains a lot of material on vyavahāra and rāja-धर्म, two of the important topics discussed by most of the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
The Rāmāyaṇa, though a kāvya or a literary composition, contains quite a few references to some of the topics discussed in the dharmaśāstra treatises. Details of the चोरोनतिओन् of a king, effects of anarchy, sins (and expiations), duties and responsi-bilities of a king, obsequial rites, value of truth, and, duties and virtues of women—all these topics have found a place in the epic, here and there.
Similarly, the Mahābhārata also contains a lot of material that comes under the purview of the धर्मशास्त्रस्. The following are the subjects dealt with, some briefly, others more exhaustively: चोरोनतिओन्, evils of anarchy, अहिṁसा (non-violence), the dharmas of the varṇas and āśramas, आचार, āpad-dharmas, पिल्ग्रिमगे, giving gifts, दायभाग, expiations for sins, rules regarding ड़ोओद्, political science (in detail), मर्रिअगे and śrāddha.
The eighteen principal पुराणस् as also some of the minor ones contain extensive and very rich material on the various topics discussed in the धर्म-śāstras. That is why the commentators and the authors of the निबन्धस् have quoted from them profusely.
A brief list of these topics as they appear in the पुराणस् may now be given:
ācāra, आह्निक, अशौच, वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas, rules about ड़ोओद्, दान, कलि-varjya (what is prohibited in the कलियुग), sins and their expiations, duties of a king, सṁस्कारस्, शान्तिस्, śrāddha, pilgrimages, vratas, vyavahāra and yugadharmas (special characteristics of the four युगस्).
Epilogue
The Hindu society has had a chequered history over the last 2500 years. The धर्मशास्त्रस् too, have grown over the same period, not only to voluminous but also to highly refined, proportions. They have played a very significant part in preserving the unity and solidarity of the society to a considerable extent.
This they have done by:
preserving the basic values of life compressed in one omnibus term called ‘dharma.’
stressing the duties and respons-ibilities towards the society much more than rights and privileges.
making the necessary adjustments to suit the needs of the changing times.
not allowing any socio-political rule to have an absolute status, but always preferring a well-established custom to the rule in the Book.
As long as there were Hindu rulers to enforce the code of conduct as prescribed by the धर्मशास्त्रस्, there was order and peace in the society. When the political power passed into the hands of ruthless alien rulers, even a safe and honourable existence became a serious problem. Hence the religious and social leaders, swimming against the current, made supreme efforts to preserve the unity and integrity of the society by modifying the आचार and the प्रायश्चित्त parts of धर्म as much as possible, since the vyavahāra part had practically passed out of their hands.
There is a charge that the writers of the धर्मशास्त्रस् of later periods (A. D. 1000 onwards) unnecessarily went into great depths to discuss small details. One should not forget that, by this time, the धर्मशास्त्रस् had become an important subject for study and discussion even in the academic circles of the day, in the traditional institutions like Maṭhas, Pāṭhaśālas and Vidyālayas. Hence, this scholarship was both necessary and useful in those circles.
Another accusation levelled against these धर्मशास्त्रस् is that they were meant only for the first three castes, that too for the ब्राह्मणस् and the क्षत्त्रिय rulers, and were not very helpful to the others. The reply is that the society of those days was like that and hence these works had to be in tune with the same. An examination of these works also reveals the startling fact that the higher a person was in the social hierarchy, more stringent were the rules guiding or binding him! And, this certainly is not a point for pointing the finger of accusation!
Again, the धर्मशास्त्रस् in general, have all along maintained that any rule disliked by the majority of the people should be replaced by a more agreeable one. The principle of कलिवर्ज्य or आपद्-धर्म is a case to the point.
After India gained political freedom, drastic changes have been made in the structure of general laws and Hindu Law, correcting many an imbalance of the past ages. In spite of this, if justice is not being meted out to the weaker sections of the society, the fault obviously lies elsewhere!

dharmayuddha
(‘war [in conformity with the principles] of धर्म’)
------------------------------------------
In spite of the desire of an overwhelming majority of the people of the world to live in peace, wars have existed, from times immemorial. Recognising it as a fact of life and even approving of it in certain circumstances, (as in the case of defending one’s territorial integrity or धर्म) the great sages of India have evolved, over the years, some general rules to be observed during the course of a battle or a war. A war fought under these rules is a ‘dharmayuddha’.
The Manusmṛti (7.90-94) gives some interesting rules. They are:
One should not use poisonous arms or deceitful means.
A foe in a disadvantageous position must not be struck.
One who has surrendered must be protected.
Those who are fleeing, the unarmed one, non-combatants or those fighting with others should not be attacked.
When रावण was worsted in his very first encounter with राम, राम let him off to return alive to his place and come back after recouping and replenishing for another round. This is a glorious example of धर्मयुद्ध.
In the कुरुक्षेत्र, the battle used to start after sunrise and stop at sunset. In the night the combatants moved freely in one another’s camps enquiring about the health and welfare of their enemies or expressing their condolences for the dead! This was a part of the धर्म-युद्ध tradition.

Dharmavyādha
------------------------------------------
Once, a ब्राह्मण who was an expert in archery, accidentally killed a sage and was cursed by him to be born as a butcher. He was reborn as the butcher धर्म-vyādha in the city of मिथिला. He was deeply devoted to his parents and served them with great fervour.
Kauśika, a ब्राह्मण mendicant, was directed by a devout होउसे-wife to learn the secrets of धर्म from धर्मव्याध of मिथिला. When कौशिक approached धर्मव्याध, he was pleased to teach him the utility and the significance of performing one’s duties in life, however unpleasant they may appear to oneself or to others. Such कर्मयोग, as it is rightly called, leads to purification of one’s मिन्द् and ultimately, to spiritual enlightenment.
His teachings—which appear in the Vanaparva of the Mahābhārata (chapters 207-216)—deserve the name ‘Vyādhagītā’.

Dharma
(‘that which supports’)
------------------------------------------
INTRODUCTION
Our scriptures are full of eulogy for धर्म. Who has not heard of the famous quotation from the Mahābhārata, ‘dharma eva hato hanti dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ,’ ‘It is धर्म that destroys (us) when destroyed; it is धर्म again that protects (us) when protected by (us)’? Or, that famous sentence put in the mouth of गान्धारी, ‘yato dharmastato jayaḥ,’ ‘Where there is धर्म, there victory also is’? Consequently we are advised in poignant terms to accumulate धर्म in our lives: ‘anityāni śarīrāṇi vibhavo naiva śāśvataḥ, nityaṁ sannihito mṛtyuḥ kartavyo धर्म-saṅgrahaḥ,’ ‘(Our) bodies are short-lived, wealth does not last long, death is constantly knocking at our door; (so) accumulation of धर्म is a must.’
WHAT IS धर्म?
What is this ‘dharma’ about which our scriptures and great men have waxed so eloquent throughout our history?
As is the case with many other Sanskrit words, it is rather difficult to give an exact translation of the word धर्म. It has been variously translated as ‘religion,’ ‘law,’ ‘duty,’ ‘religious ordinance or rite,’ ‘code of conduct’ and so on. It can mean anyone or more or all of these, depending upon the context. The reason seems to be that the word itself has been used in various senses down the ages and its meaning as also scope has been enlarged. It will be worthwhile to study this development.
It is universally accepted that the word धर्म comes from the root ‘dhṛ’ (‘to uphold,’ ‘to support,’ ‘to sustain’). An oftquoted verse from the Mahābhārata says: ‘dhāraṇāt dharmam ityāhuḥ dharmo dhārayate prajāḥ,’ ‘They call it धर्म since it upholds; it is धर्म that upholds the people (of the world).’
That which upholds this created universe, supports it and sustains it, without which the universe just falls apart, is धर्म. Viewed from this standpoint, धर्म is none other than God Himself. It is what the उपनिषद्स् describe as sat or tat, the very essence of one’s being. Whatever conduct or way of life helps us to reveal this fundamental principle in us, can also be called धर्म, though in a secondary sense. Hence religious rites, ceremonies and observances, fixed principles of conduct, privileges, duties and obligations of a man depending upon his stage of life and status in society, even rules of law, customs and manners of society—everyone of these can be included under the term धर्म.
ṚTA AND SATYA
It may be interesting and instructive to turn our attention to two more ancient words, ṛta and सत्य, which are closely connected with, if not forms of, धर्म. The word ṛta has been used profusely in the वेदस्, especially in the Ṛgveda and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. The word in its simplest form, seems to indicate a straight or direct line and so, universal laws of nature, an impersonal order. When extended to the moral world, it denotes a straight conduct based on truth which itself is also धर्म. It has also been used in the sense of an inner awareness of what is true, based on the scriptural teachings and the needs of the duties on hand. When this awareness expresses itself through words and actions, it becomes सत्य. Thus we see that the meanings of all the three words more or less coalesce.
DHARMA AS THE FOUNDATION OF THE WORLD
Since everything in this world appears to have a beginning and an end, with an intervening period of existence, it is but natural for the human intelligence to conceive of a beginning for this च्रेअतिओन् and to posit an eternal God who existed before च्रेअतिओन् and from whom च्रेअतिओन् proceeded. For instance: ‘sadeva somyeda-magra āsīt, ekamevādvitīyam... tadaikṣata bahu syām prajāyeya iti,’ ‘My dear (boy), in the beginning Sat alone existed, the One without a second. It reflected, “May I become many! May I be born!” ’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1-3). The ‘many’ that were created, needed a central integrating force, a law or a principle; for, otherwise, chaos would result. This law or principle is धर्म. Even this was created by God himself: ‘tat śreyorūpam asṛjata dharmam... tasmāt dharmāt param nāsti... yo vai sa dharmaḥ satyaṁ vai tat,’ ‘He specially created that धर्म, of the form of the highest good... therefore there is nothing higher than that... that धर्म is verily सत्य’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.14). This धर्म is the firm foundation upon which the entire universe stands (‘dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā’—Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 79.7). Obviously here, धर्म means righteous behaviour based on truth and knowledge of the unity in spite of the diversity, and capable of bringing the highest good to the whole च्रेअतिओन्. All other meanings, senses and derivations of this in later literature are corollaries of this central idea.
DHARMA AS DUTIES
The word धर्म occurs in the Ṛgveda fifty-six times (e.g., 5.63.7; 5.72.2; 9.7.1; 9.25.2; 10.88.1; 10.170.2). But in almost all these places it has been used in the sense of duty or action which contributes to the sustenance of the world (‘jagad-dhāraka-कर्म’). In the उपनिषद्स्, this sense becomes more explicit. As a member of the society each one of us has certain duties and obligations which must be discharged by performing the prescribed actions. This sustains the structure of the society. Similarly, in our journey towards perfection we have to pass through several stages of spiritual development and each such stage devolves upon us certain duties or a code of conduct. This helps to sustain our inner development and simultaneously contributes to the well-being of the society also. The seeds of this—which is well-known as वर्ण-आश्रम-धर्म in later literature—are to be found in the Puruṣasūkta and in the earlier उपनिषद्स् also. For instance, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka passage already quoted (1.4.14) there is clear reference to धर्म as a force that regulates even a क्षत्त्रिय, who by virtue of his position as a ruler, could misuse his powers for self-aggrandizement. In the famous passage of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (2.31.1) the reference to the duties of āśramas is crystal clear: ‘trayo dharmaskandhā yajño’dhyayanaṁ dānamiti prathamaḥ...’ ‘Dharma has three branches. Performance of sacrifice, study of scriptures and giving gifts—this is the first.’
DHARMA IN THE UPANIṢADS
Sometimes, the word धर्म has also been used in the उपनिषद्स् in the sense of अपूर्व of the Pūrva Mīmāṁsā System (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.11—‘ayaṁ dharmaḥ sarveṣām bhūtānām मधु’). This अपूर्व is nothing but the subtle effect of an action performed as per the directions of the scriptures, which will produce suitable results later.
In rare cases, the word has also been used to denote the आत्मन् or the Self: ‘aṇureṣa dharmaḥ,’ ‘This Self is very subtle’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.21); ‘evaṁ dharmān pṛthak paśyan,’ ‘thus, considering the selves to be separate’ (i.e., ‘different in different bodies’) (ibid 4.14).
In the Ācāryopadeśa of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, the word धर्म has been clearly used in the sense of obligatory works: ‘dharmaṁ cara,’ ‘Perform your ordained actions’ (1.11.1).
DHARMA IN THE GĪTĀ
Coming to the Bhagavadgītā, we find the term used in a more definite and clear sense. धर्म is righteousness, the basis of all पुरुषार्थस् (18.34). It is one’s duty ordained by the scriptures as per one’s वर्ण and आश्रम, by properly performing which, man attains both well-being in this world (abhyudaya) and highest good (niśśreyasa) (vide 4.8; 18.31; 1.40; 7.11 etc.). Sometimes it has also been used as synonymous with आत्मज्ञान (vide 9.3) or with कर्मयोग (2.40).
DHARMA IN THE RĀMĀYAṆA
Let us now turn to the two epics. The very name Rāmāyaṇa has been explained as ‘rāmasya ayanaṁ vṛttaṁ caritam,’ ‘the path trodden by राम or the conduct of राम.’ Śrī राम is the hero here, depicted as the ideal man. His conduct was in perfect conformity with धर्म as taught and understood then. To such an extent did he go that he has been described by the sage वाल्मीकि as ‘rāmo vigrahavān dharmaḥ,’ ‘Rāma is धर्म personified’. To speak the truth and to keep up the promise given, under all circumstances—this is the keynote of धर्म in the Rāmāyaṇa. No hardship is too great, no sacrifice is too great, when compared to the fulfilment of this धर्म. राम had the full power and strength to vanquish दशरथ or anybody else and anoint himself as the king. Yet he did not do it since he was afraid of अधर्म (Rāmāyaṇa 2.53.26). To please his ड़थेर् and help him keep up his promise to कैकेयी he was prepared to jump into the fire or consume deadly poison or drown himself in the ocean (ibid., 2.18.28-29). He was ready to give up his life or सीता or even लक्ष्मण but would never break the promise once made (ibid., 3.10.19). He was not at all hesitant to forsake even सीता in order to set up a very high standard of family life. Since his observance of धर्म was dynamic, we can safely surmise that he set up new norms of धर्म by accepting the होस्पितलित्य् of गुह and शबरी, by refusing to have more than one wife and by forcing विभीषण to conduct the last rites of रावण.
DHARMA IN THE MAHĀBHĀRATA
The Mahābhārata is a veritable encyclopaedia of धर्म. It is here that the well-known definition of धर्म (‘dhāraṇād dharmamityāhuḥ’) already quoted, occurs. The epic gives a detailed delineation of the varṇāśrama-dharmas. The dhārmic virtues like सत्य and अहिṁसा are highly extolled. Performance of ordained duties, however small or mean or repulsive they may appear to be, is recommended and eulogised through the stories of धर्मव्याध, तुलाधार and the simple housewife. The idea of the four पुरुषार्थस् is well-developed, giving worldly life and worldly pursuits a decent place in the scheme of life. Another very interesting feature of this epic is the relaxation of the well-known moral standards and norms in times of distress and emergencies (termed as आपद्-धर्म) which bespeaks of the robust common sense of the author of the epic.
DHARMA IN MĪMĀṀSĀ AND VAIŚEṢIKA SYSTEMS
It may not be out of place here to refer to two more interpretations of धर्म. जैमिनि in his Pūrvamīmāṁsā Sūtras (1.1.2) uses the word in a very restricted sense: ‘codanā-lakṣaṇo’rtho dharmaḥ,’ ‘Dharma is the desirable goal or result that is indicated by injunctive (Vedic) passages’. So, धर्म means the Vedic ritualistic actions leading to happiness here or hereafter. कणाद on the other hand, gives a more liberal definition: “yato’bhyudaya-niśśreyasa-siddhiḥ sa dharmaḥ,” ‘Dharma is that from which will result both worldly well-being and final beatitude’ (Vaiśeṣika Sūtras 1.2).
DHARMA IN SMṚTIS AND DHARMAŚĀSTRAS
However it is in the smṛtis that we come across a very detailed treatment of the subject of धर्म in all its intricacies. That is why they have been rightly designated as ‘Dharmaśāstras.’ If धर्म is the Cosmic Law which holds together the beings of the world and sustains them, it is very necessary that they be given detailed practical instructions about the way of life which helps them to be always in step and in tune with this धर्म. Since human beings, like animals, are gregarious by nature, these instructions naturally have to have a sociological bias. This is exactly what the धर्मशास्त्रस् have done when they delineate the वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas. True to the tradition of our motherland, all the धर्मशास्त्रस् owe their allegiance to the वेदस्. In addition, they also accept the words and conduct of saints, sages and seers well-versed in the knowledge of the वेदस्, as authoritative in determining धर्म (vide Manusmṛti 2.6; Gautama Dharmasūtras 1.1-2; Āpastamba Dharmasūtras 1.1.1.2; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.7).
Since man is a rational being and since life-situations are sometimes quite intriguing, the धर्मशास्त्रस् wisely recognised the need for reflective मोरलित्य् also, as for instance in Yājñavalkya Smṛti (1.7): ‘śrutiḥ smṛtiḥ sadācāraḥ svasya ca priyamātmanaḥ samyaksaṅkalpajaḥ kāmo dharmamūlam idaṁ smṛtam,’ ‘The वेदस्, smṛtis, usages of good men, what is agreeable to one’s self and desire born of deliberation—these are traditionally recognised as the source of धर्म’.
Hinduism considers man’s life as a long journey towards perfection. In this journey, natural desires and inclinations of man to possess and enjoy the good things of life cannot be overlooked. Hence the धर्मशास्त्रस् provide for these in their scheme of life while amplifying the theory of the पुरुषार्थस्. Great care has been taken to give detailed rules and regulations in the acquisition of अर्थ (wealth) and काम (enjoyment of fleshly desires) within the framework of धर्म. However, following in the footsteps of the Jñānakāṇḍa (section that deals with spiritual wisdom) of the वेदस्, they always stress the importance of trying for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् as the summum bonum of life (vide Manusmṛti 12.116 to 125).
No society under the sun is absolutely homogeneous. Differences do exist. Even the five fingers of our own hand exhibit this principle. The धर्मशास्त्रस् recognised this natural division, called it God-made and gave detailed instructions regarding the duties and responsibilities of various groups or varṇas of society towards one another in their group and towards other groups. Stressing that these divisions were evolved due to गुण (quality) and कर्म (vocation), they have also provided for stringent punishments for derelictions of duty and rewards for sincere performance. Relaxations of these rules have however been provided for, in times of distress.
While dealing with the duties of a king, the धर्मशास्त्रस् have given us a fairly well-developed form of Indian Jurisprudence. Fairness and justice occupy the central place in all these rules (vide Manusmṛti, chapters 8 & 9).
In consonance with the same principle that life is a long journey towards perfection, stations (āśramas) have been provided in a man’s life for effecting this perfection gradually. Detailed directions have been provided with regard to each of the āśramas.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् have not forgotten to provide for some basic rules common to all the varṇas and āśramas (sāmānya-dharmas). A perusal of these will reveal to us the great stress laid on the moral life.
To err is human, to forgive divine. For the Divine to forgive, the human being must make himself pure by recognising his own sins and repenting for them. The धर्मशास्त्रस् have given us a detailed treatment of the various kinds of sins and necessary expiations or prāyaścittas (vide Manusmṛti, chapters 10 & 11; Yājñavalkya Smṛti, 3.205 to 327; Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtras, chapters 20 to 28).
Apart from these, the धर्मशास्त्रस् also deal with the सṁस्कारस् or sacraments which purify human beings, making them better fitted for the spiritual journey in life.
We thus see that the concept of धर्म has undergone a healthy evolution over the years, always keeping to the core meaning.
DHARMA, NOT A STAGNANT CONCEPT
Sometimes it is alleged that the Hindu society is very conservative and its धर्म (as social laws, customs and manners) is outmoded and stagnant. An impartial study of the smṛtis shows, on the other hand, that social laws have been constantly changed, depending on the needs of the times. Even मनु and याज्ञवल्क्य, the earliest smṛtikāras, say that when a धर्म (a law or rule or custom) is hated or disliked by people (lokavikṛta) it must be given up (vide Manu 4.176). Throughout the social history of India we find the rules and regulations being changed to suit the tastes and needs of the people, though of course, the central spiritual principles have always been kept intact. Criticism of Vedic ritualism by the उपनिषद्स्, changes in the views regarding अनुलोम marriages 1 and ड़ोओद्, the कलि-varjya principle कलि. For instance, animal sacrifice in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.">2—all these clearly show that the Hindu sages and law-givers were endowed with immense common sense and that the Hindu society had always been dynamic.
CONCLUSION
Thus the history of धर्म from the most ancient days up to the modern period shows that it has always been dynamic and a very real force to reckon with in the life of our nation.
We have seen how धर्म which was conceived of as the Cosmic Law was gradually metamorphosed into duties and responsibilities prescribed for various beings in different stages of evolution in life, but always based on the principle that this evolution should ultimately bring about spiritual enlightenment. If this fact is kept in मिन्द् and all the members of the society act according to धर्म, there is no reason why all should not live in happiness and peace. After all, the saying, ‘dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ’ of the great ṛṣi व्यास cannot go in vain!

Dharmasūtras
------------------------------------------
The धर्मसूत्रस् are the third aspect or branch of the Kalpasūtra literature, the last of the six वेदाङ्गस् (subsidiary sciences of the वेदस्). Also known as the Sāmayācārika sūtras, they deal mainly with आचार and vyavahāra (code of conduct in personal and social life) as also the varṇāśramadharmas.
Though the गृह्यसूत्रस् and the धर्मसूत्रस् are closely connected and the topics are sometimes overlapped, the former confines itself mainly to pākayajñas and सṁस्कारस् (See VEDIC SACRIFICES and SAṀSKĀRAS.) whereas the latter, to varṇāśramadharmas.

dharmabhūtajñāna
(‘knowledge [which is an] attribute [of the Self]’)
------------------------------------------
How the jīvātman or the individual सोउल् knows an object, whether such know-ledge or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is accidental to it or innate to it, is a subject of discussion in the darśanas or Indian philosophical systems.
If the Advaita Vedānta posits the view that चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is the very nature of the सोउल्, the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta as expounded by Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) asserts that ज्ञान or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is always present in ईश्वर or God and the जीव or the सोउल् as their धर्म or attribute.
This धर्मभूतज्ञान or attributive चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is ‘ajaḍa’ (non-material and also non-spiritual). It illumines itself and other objects. It always exists for another and never for itself. That is, it cannot know itself, but illumines objects for the conscious subject for whom it is an attribute.
This धर्मभूतज्ञान is eternal and all-pervasive in the case of ईश्वर, the nityasūris (eternally illumined souls) and the liberated souls. However, in the case of the jīvātman (the सोउल् in bondage) it is contracted or obscured. When the jīvātman realises the beatific form of the Divine through the yogas of कर्म, ज्ञान and भक्ति, his धर्मभूतज्ञान also expands to infinity and becomes perfect.
Terms such as mati, prajñā, saṁvit and śemuṣī are all synonyms of धर्म-bhūtajñāna.

dharmaskandha
(‘branch of धर्म’)
------------------------------------------
This is an expression peculiar only to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (2.23.1).
‘Skandha’ means a division. ‘Dharma’ means a way of life. The three ways of life mentioned are those of the householder, the forest-dweller and the Vedic student.
The householder keeps and tends the Vedic fires, and, performs sacrifices. He also studies the वेदस् to retain the knowledge he has already gained. Giving gifts to the needy is his another duty. He is the first धर्मस्कन्ध.
The forest-dweller (as also the mendi-cant) is meant by the word ‘tapas’ or austerity, because he leads an austere life. He is the second धर्मस्कन्ध.
The Vedic student entirely devoted to the study of the scriptures and service to the गुरु is the next, the third धर्म-skandha.
According to this Upaniṣad, all of them (after death) go to puṇyalokas or heavenly regions attainable by religious merit.

Dharmarājaratha
------------------------------------------
Situated at a distance of about 50 kms. (31 miles) from the city of Madras (now called ‘Chennai’), on an open beach, is the village महाबलिपुरम् or Māmalla-puram, by name. It has carved for itself an important place in the archaeological map of India since it contains ancient rock-cut temples called ‘Rathas,’ belonging to the period A. D. 670 to 700 and built by the Pallava king Rājasiṁha, also known as Narasiṁhavarman.
These Rathas, seven of them, have withstood the vagaries of time and weather, since they have been cut in granite and in single blocks or big boulders. The धर्मराजरथ is the biggest of them. (A ‘ratha’ is a chariot or a temple-car, the same as a विमान or the shrine of the temple.)
This रथ is almost a square structure, measuring 8 metres by 8 metres and rising up to 10.5 meters (26 ft. square and 35 ft. in height). It has three storeys including the ground floor. There are a number of images of Hindu gods like शिव, ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, Ardhanārīśvara, नरसिṁह and Varāha. Over these images are short epigraphs containing the name of the king who built the रथ.
This रथ too, as the others, seems to be incomplete. It looks as though the construction was suddenly stopped.

dhāraṇā
(‘fixing [the मिन्द्]’)
------------------------------------------
Controlling the vagaries of one’s मिन्द् and concentrating it on a particular subject has been a life-time’s ambition for many a cultured human being. पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.), the ancient teacher of योग, has given us enough material and guidance in this regard in his incomparable work, the Yogasūtras.
Out of the eight standard steps he recommends, धारणा is the sixth. It is the fixing of attention on a definite locus, such as the lotus of the heart (imagining a red, twelve-petalled, lotus in the region of the heart for purposes of meditation), the light in the brain (imagining a brilliant light in the crown of the head), on the tip of the nose or the tongue, or on an external object like the मोओन् or the image of a god and so on.
It is natural for the fickle मिन्द् to get distracted and run away from this object of concentration. However, it is to be repeatedly brought back through strenuous efforts until it develops into ध्यान or continuous flow (of the मिन्द्) towards the object.
See YOGADARŚANA for details.

Dharmasthala
------------------------------------------
This is a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे very popular among the people of Karnataka State. It is situated at a distance of 75 kms. (46 miles) to the east of the city of Mangalore, near the west coast. The river Netrāvatī flows close by.
धर्मस्थल">Mañjunātheśvara Temple at DharmasthalaThis place was originally known as Kuḍuma (or Koḍuma). According to the local legends, a pious Jain couple who lived here, were commanded by four dharmadevatās—Kālarāhu, Kālarakāi, Kumārasvāmi and Kanyākumārī—to establish a temple for themselves, which was done. Later on, a शिव temple with a लिङ्ग was also built. Sometime during A. D. 1513 वादिराज (A. D. 1480-1600), a great saint of the Sode मठ of the Mādhva tradition, arrived here. He re-established the लिङ्ग at the शिव temple with proper rites and named the town as धर्मस्थल. The descendants of the original Jain couple, with the surname Heggaḍe (or Pergaḍe), are the धर्म-darśis (chief trustees) of the whole complex.
The temple of Śiva—now known as Mañjunātheśvara—is the central shrine and the chief attraction of the pilgrims. The main doors are covered with silver plates. The four corners have four small kalaśas or pinions.
The worship in this main temple is managed by the Vaiṣṇava ब्राह्मणस् of the Mādhva tradition.
The following are the major festivals observed in this temple: Lakṣadīpotsava in the month of Kārttika (November); Gaṇeśacaturthī; Mahāśivarātri; दीपावली; nine-day festival during Meṣa-सङ्क्रान्ति (in April) including रथोत्सव (temple-car-festival) and worship of Divine मोथेर् during Navarātri (October).
There are smaller temples dedicated to the four dharmadevatās and Aṇṇappa (a benevolent spirit).
The huge stone image of Bāhubali, a great saint of जैनिस्म्, is another attraction of this place. It is nearly 12 metres (39 ft.) high and is mounted on a pedestal of 4 metres (11 ft.). It was installed in A. D. 1982.
The large campus has several guest houses and excellent arrangements to feed the thousands of pilgrims that constantly throng the place.
People of all religions visit this pilgrim centre in large numbers maintaining perfect peace and harmony.
The management is running a large number of educational and public utility institutions spread all over the Karnataka State.
